Professional Termite Control in Wichita, KS: Treatment Options That Actually Work

If you're searching for termite control Wichita KS, you've likely spotted mud tubes on your foundation, heard about termites from a home inspector, or you're buying property and need a Wood Destroying Insect (WDI) report. Whatever brought you here, you're dealing with a problem that causes $5 billion in property damage across the United States every year — and Kansas homeowners aren't immune. At Shaw's Pest Control, we've been protecting homes from termites since 1987. Dave Shaw holds three state certifications and a Master Tech Certification, and in over 35 years, he's treated every level of termite infestation across Wichita, El Dorado, Derby, Andover, and surrounding areas. This page covers the termite threats facing south-central Kansas homes, the three treatment methods we use, and what you should know before choosing a provider.

Why Subterranean Termites Are the Dominant Threat in Kansas

Kansas is home to subterranean termites — underground foragers that live in massive colonies in the soil and enter your home through cracks in the foundation, gaps around plumbing, or even through treated wood if the barrier has weakened. Unlike drywood termites that live inside the wood itself, subterranean termites tunnel back and forth between the soil (where they get moisture) and your home (where they find food). That means they're nearly invisible for years. You won't see them chewing through your floor joists or wall studs until the damage is already severe.

Butler and Sedgwick County have clay-heavy, moisture-retaining soil that creates ideal conditions for termite colonies. The soil stays damp longer after rains, and that consistent moisture lets colonies thrive year-round, even through Kansas winters. That's why professional termite control in Wichita focuses on creating a treated barrier between the soil and the structure — because that's where the threat originates.

Shaw's Three Termite Treatment Options: Bait, Liquid, and Hybrid

We tailor every termite treatment to the property, the level of infestation, and the homeowner's goals. Here's how each method works.

1. Advance Termite Bait System (Preferred Method)

The Advance Termite Bait System is our most commonly recommended solution for active termite control and long-term prevention. Here's how it works: we install bait stations in the soil around the perimeter of your home, spaced 10–20 feet apart depending on the structure and landscape. Each station contains a monitoring device. Termites foraging underground find the stations, feed on the bait, and carry it back to the colony. The active ingredient disrupts the termites' ability to molt, which eliminates the colony over time — not just the workers you see, but the entire population including the queen.

This system is designed for colony elimination, not just suppression. It's also non-invasive (no drilling through slabs or trenching around the foundation), and it provides ongoing monitoring. We check and refresh the stations during scheduled visits, which means you're not just treating a current problem — you're preventing future infestations.

2. Liquid Soil Treatment

Liquid termiticide treatments create a continuous chemical barrier in the soil around and beneath your foundation. We trench around the perimeter of the home, apply a liquid termiticide to the soil, and then backfill. For homes with basements or crawl spaces, we treat the interior perimeter as well. The goal is to establish a treated zone that termites cannot cross without contacting the product, which either repels or kills them on contact.

This method is fast-acting and effective for homes with active infestations that need immediate intervention. The products we use are industry-leading, non-repellent formulas that termites can't detect — so they move through the treated zone, pick up the product, and spread it throughout the colony. Liquid treatments typically last 5–10 years depending on soil conditions and the product used.

3. Hybrid Treatment for Severe Infestations

In cases of severe or widespread infestation — especially in older homes, properties with multiple structural entry points, or homes near wooded areas — we recommend a hybrid approach that combines both liquid soil treatment and bait stations. The liquid treatment provides immediate knockdown and establishes a protective barrier, while the bait system targets any remaining colony activity and provides ongoing monitoring. This is the most comprehensive option, and it's what we use when a homeowner wants absolute confidence that the problem is solved and won't return.

If you're in Augusta or another outlying area with older construction or known termite pressure, this combination approach is worth considering.

What a Shaw's Termite Inspection Includes

Whether you're buying a home, refinancing, or just concerned about what you've seen, a professional termite inspection is the first step. Here's what Dave and the Shaw's team look for during an inspection:

  • Mud tubes: Pencil-width tunnels on foundation walls, floor joists, or crawl space piers — these are the termites' highways between the soil and the wood.
  • Hollow-sounding wood: Termites eat wood from the inside out, so damaged wood sounds hollow when tapped and may feel soft or crumble under pressure.
  • Swarmer termites or discarded wings: Reproductive termites swarm in the spring. If you see winged termites indoors or piles of wings near windowsills, that's a red flag.
  • Frass (termite droppings): Though more common with drywood termites, any sign of insect waste near wood is worth investigating.
  • Moisture damage or wood rot: Termites are drawn to moisture. Leaky pipes, poor drainage, or damp crawl spaces make your home more attractive.

We provide detailed written reports, and for real estate transactions, we can issue official WDI (Wood Destroying Insect) reports required by lenders. Learn more about what goes into a thorough evaluation on our post about termite inspection cost.

If you're concerned about early warning signs, check out our guide on signs of termite infestation.

Termite Pressure in El Dorado and South-Central Kansas

Termite activity isn't uniform across the country. In drier climates like Arizona or Nevada, subterranean termite pressure is lower because colonies struggle to find consistent moisture. But here in south-central Kansas — especially in Butler and Sedgwick counties — our clay-heavy soils retain water longer, creating the perfect environment for termite colonies to grow and spread. Homes in El Dorado, Wichita, Derby, and Andover are all in high-risk zones.

That doesn't mean every home will get termites, but it does mean prevention and early detection matter. An annual inspection program can catch termite activity before it becomes structural damage. Dave Shaw has seen it all in 35+ years — from minor infestations caught early to homes with compromised floor systems that required major repairs. The difference almost always comes down to timing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does termite treatment take?

Most termite treatments can be completed in one day. Bait station installation typically takes 2–4 hours depending on the size of the property. Liquid soil treatments may take longer if trenching around the entire foundation is required, especially for larger homes or those with landscaping obstacles. Shaw's will provide a time estimate during the inspection.

How soon can termites return after treatment?

With proper treatment and follow-up monitoring, termites should not return for many years. Liquid treatments last 5–10 years depending on soil conditions. Bait systems provide ongoing colony elimination and monitoring as long as the stations are maintained. Without annual inspections or preventive measures, however, new colonies can establish themselves over time, especially in high-pressure areas like Wichita.

Do I need annual termite service?

Annual service isn't legally required, but it's highly recommended. Termites don't go away on their own, and new colonies can move into treated areas over time. An annual inspection catches early warning signs before they become expensive problems. Many homeowners also choose annual bait station monitoring, which provides continuous protection and peace of mind. You can learn more about long-term prevention in our post on how to prevent termites.

What does a termite inspection cost?

Termite inspection costs vary depending on the size of the property and whether you need a formal WDI report for a real estate transaction. Shaw's Pest Control offers competitive pricing and often provides free inspections with treatment. Contact us at (316) 251-9461 for a quote specific to your property.

Is termite treatment safe for my foundation?

Yes. Modern termite treatments — both liquid and bait-based — are designed to be safe for your foundation, your home's structure, and your family. Liquid termiticides are applied to the soil, not directly to the foundation material itself, and they do not degrade concrete, brick, or stone. Bait systems are installed in the ground around the perimeter and pose no risk to the structure. Shaw's uses only proven, industry-standard products and follows all manufacturer guidelines and Kansas state regulations.
